card.hook: Every hour, a trumpet call drifts down from the taller tower of St. Mary's and then stops mid-tune. Don't worry, nobody forgot the ending. It's a good cue to get your phone out.
card.stand_here: Stand out in Rynek Główny, on the northeastern corner of the Main Market Square near ul. Floriańska. Face the basilica and step back until both towers fit, with the Cloth Hall (Sukiennice) in the frame too.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the basilica and the Cloth Hall into one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural look at the church, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the tower tops and the gilded crown.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line a tower up with a vertical line and keep your phone level, so the towers stand tall instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Early morning is the sweet spot, when the square is nearly empty and the basilica is lit from the east. Around the top of the hour, film a short clip to catch the trumpet call.
card.selfie_here: Walk onto ul. Floriańska, stand on the paved street and face away from the basilica so its towers rise in the distance behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and let the street's facades frame you. For a close-up, the small Plac Mariacki beside the church puts the facade right behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand under the Cloth Hall arches on the Main Square and frame you with the whole basilica behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The basilica is a working church, and photos inside need a photo permit, so check the official site before you go. If the facade looks partly covered, that may be building work (the towers were reported under repair in summer 2025), so take a few frames from different spots.
card.challenge: Frame the tower through the Cloth Hall arches so the gap makes a picture frame, then see if a friend can guess where you took it.
card.good_to_know: The basilica is about 80 m tall, and its two towers are different heights. The church dates from the 14th century, though its foundations go back to the early 13th. Inside, there's a carved wooden altarpiece by Veit Stoss.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand out in Rynek Główny, on the northeastern corner of the Main Market Square near ul. Floriańska. Face the basilica and step back until both towers fit, with the Cloth Hall (Sukiennice) in the frame too.

card.hook: Wawel does not do subtle. The pale walls, towers and rooftops sit up on their limestone hill like they know you're about to take a photo, and from the right spot they all line up as one skyline.
card.stand_here: Stand about 85 m north-east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, near Mała Baszta, and face south-west. That way the walls and rooflines fill your frame, so step back a few paces if the top gets cut off.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the main view of the castle. If you're close and want the walls and towers in one frame, drop to zoom 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for roofs, turrets and windows.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line a tower or roofline up with a horizontal line, so the tall walls look straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the walls and fewer people in your shot. In the evening, try night mode and hold the phone very still.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the far end of Kanonicza Street, where the castle fills the background. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep Wawel over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Cross Grunwaldzki Bridge and go down on the right to the Vistula riverbank, where the castle is straight ahead. Ask a passer-by to stand on the bank while you stand in front of them, with the castle in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Parts of the castle and its exhibitions are likely to need tickets and have visiting rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole castle, then find three details to zoom in on: a roof edge, a window and a tower. Bonus points if you also track down the fire-breathing dragon statue by the river.
card.good_to_know: King Casimir III the Great ordered the castle begun, and the current building dates from the 14th century. Many generations added to it, so it gathers around a Renaissance courtyard and mixes medieval, Renaissance and Baroque styles. Wawel Cathedral, where Polish monarchs were crowned and buried, stands right beside it.

card.hook: Don't expect drama from the front of this building. It's plain and honest, and it still looks much as it did in the 1940s, which is why a simple photo works so well here.
card.stand_here: Stand on ulica Lipowa, on the street side, directly opposite the front of number 4. Face the building and keep the whole width of the facade in view, with the entrance gate in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which gives the most natural-looking facade. Switch to 0.5x only if the street is too narrow to fit the whole front in, and keep the building centred so the edges don't stretch. Try zoom 2x if you want a close-up of the gate.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the building up with the vertical lines so the walls don't lean, and keep the phone level rather than pointing it up.
card.best_time: Daylight is best for reading the facade clearly. Earlier in the day is likely to be quieter at the gate, but check how the light falls on the front when you arrive.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the pavement in front of the facade and entrance gate at Lipowa 4, with the building behind you over your shoulder. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it so the building fills the frame behind you. Keep it low-key, since this is a serious place.
card.rules_and_safety: You can see the facade and gate from the street without a ticket. The museum inside is ticketed and the courtyard isn't open public space, so check the official site for tickets, opening times and photo rules. Listings say personal photos are allowed in the exhibition with the flash off.
card.challenge: Can you get the whole front in one shot with every vertical line dead straight, and no leaning walls?
card.good_to_know: Oskar Schindler took over the factory in 1939 and renamed it Deutsche Emailwarenfabrik in January 1940. The number of Jewish workers grew from just over 150 in 1940 to around 1,100 by 1944. Today the site holds a branch of the Historical Museum of the City of Kraków, whose exhibition on Kraków under occupation has been here since 2007, and the Museum of Contemporary Art in Kraków in the former workshops.

card.hook: Imagine the city pulling down its medieval walls and planting a 4 km ring of gardens in their place. That's Planty, and it makes a very relaxed backdrop for your holiday snaps.
card.stand_here: Stand at Brama Floriańska, on the Planty walk just outside the Florian Gate, and look back along the park. Planty Park lies to the north-west.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the gate and the tree-lined paths fit nicely. Switch to 0.5x if you want more of the leafy arch overhead, or try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the gate's details from further back.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the gate on one of the vertical lines, then tap the gate and slide a little darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the stone and leaves.
card.best_time: Early in the day is likely to be quieter on the paths. Flowers, autumn colour and fog all change the look through the year, so any season can surprise you.
card.selfie_here: Head to the little wrought-iron bridge over the pond in the garden by the Barbican, and stand with the planted garden behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more greenery in, and keep your arm a touch higher so the garden shows.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone on the Planty walkway between the Barbican and the Florian Gate and ask them to step far enough back to fit both gates and the park in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Planty is an open public park. The Barbican may be closed at times, but you don't need to go inside for these views.
card.challenge: Let the path run from the bottom of your frame to the gate, with a tree trunk on each side, and wait for a gap in the walkers to get a path that's all yours.
card.good_to_know: Planty was laid out between 1822 and 1830 on the line of the old defensive walls. It covers about 21 hectares as a chain of thirty smaller gardens. The Florian Gate and the Barbican beside it survived, and the Barbican is one of only three fortified outposts of its kind still standing in Europe.

card.hook: Picture a six-metre bronze dragon on a big rock, and a crowd of people all holding their phones up, waiting for it to burp fire. Join them, because it's a lot more fun than it sounds.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Bulwar Czerwieński riverbank walkway below Wawel Hill, where you can see the statue from the path. Face the dragon so the western face of the castle rises behind it and the Vistula is beside it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the dragon, the castle and the river into one frame. Switch to 1x for a balanced shot, then 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for a tighter shot of the head and flame.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the dragon, then slide the brightness down a little so the flame doesn't turn into a white blob.
card.best_time: There's no proven best time of day. If you want flame in your shot, wait for it, because it comes on by itself every few minutes. The timing varies, and it's sometimes switched off for maintenance.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera on the Bulwar Czerwieński walkway, and turn so the castle's western face is over your shoulder. For a fire selfie, stand right at the statue by the Dragon's Den exit and time it for the flame, though the dragon will be in front of you, not behind.
card.ask_someone: For a wider shot with you in it, ask someone on the Vistula boulevard across the river, roughly below the Sheraton Hotel, while you stand by the dragon.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep a safe distance when the flames appear, especially if you're with children. The dragon's den cave is a separate ticketed, seasonal visit, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Catch the exact moment the flame starts, with your best 'I'm totally not scared' face in the corner.
card.good_to_know: This is the star of Krakow's best-known legend: a dragon terrorised the town until a cobbler named Skuba tricked it into drinking so much river water that it burst. Sculptor Bronisław Chromy designed the statue, finished it in 1969, and it was placed here in 1972. It sits on a large limestone boulder, and you can also set off the flame by text message.

card.hook: The best view of Wawel Cathedral isn't from up on the hill. It's from down by the water, where the Vistula bends and the whole castle skyline gets a second copy in the reflection.
card.stand_here: Stand on Bulwar Czerwieński, the riverside boulevard at the foot of Wawel Hill, and face the castle across the water. The cathedral sits to the east, on top of the hill.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x for a low, wide view of the hill, river and reflection. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick the cathedral out from the rest of the castle, and use 1x when you want a balanced, natural look.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the waterline on the lower third, so the river fills the bottom and the reflection has room.
card.best_time: Go at sunset, when the water mirrors the castle and the light is softest. As it fades, switch on night mode.
card.selfie_here: Head to the open grass in front of the cathedral complex on Wawel Hill, or the garden beside the Wawel visitor center (check it on your map). Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and hold the phone a bit low so the cathedral rises over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot you from the riverside boulevard below the hill, with you in front and the whole hill and cathedral behind you, ideally at golden hour.
card.rules_and_safety: The boulevard is open public space, but the cathedral is a place of worship. Check the official Wawel site before you go for access and photography rules, especially for the royal tombs and crypts.
card.challenge: Get the waterline on the lower third with the skyline above it, then see if you can spot the golden dome in your shot.
card.good_to_know: The cathedral is nearly 1,000 years old, and the Gothic building you see today is the third church on this spot. It was consecrated in 1364, and from 1320 until 1764 Polish monarchs were crowned here. Rulers kept adding chapels, so you'll spot Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque touches, with golden-domed Sigismund's Chapel the best known.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Bulwar Czerwieński, the riverside boulevard at the foot of Wawel Hill, and face the castle across the water. The cathedral sits to the east, on top of the hill.

card.hook: Picture a square so big that the whole Cloth Hall sits in the middle of it like a giant loaf on a table, with two uneven church towers watching over it. That's Kraków's Main Square, and the trick is knowing which corner to stand in.
card.stand_here: Stand at the northeast corner of the square, where Floriańska Street meets Rynek Główny. Face into the square and you'll see St Mary's Basilica and the Cloth Hall (Sukiennice) sitting together in one frame, the classic postcard view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the basilica and the Cloth Hall in together. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out details on the basilica towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the Cloth Hall along the lower third, then tap the basilica facade and slide it a touch darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning, around 7-8 AM, is lovely: the light falls well on the basilica facade and the square is quiet.
card.selfie_here: Grab a selfie at the Adam Mickiewicz Monument in the middle of the square: use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the basilica in over your shoulder. For something more playful, the bronze Eros Bound head sculpture beside the Town Hall Tower is a popular selfie spot, and you can climb inside it. Tilt yourself to shoot it face-on.
card.ask_someone: Stand across from the Chopin Restaurant with the basilica and the Cloth Hall behind you, and ask a passer-by to shoot from the other side, away from the middle of the square.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside the basilica is restricted, and its visit page suggests skipping flash and selfie sticks in there (advice, not a formal ban). The Town Hall Tower and basilica tower are separate paid visits, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Keep your phone perfectly level so the buildings don't lean, then see if you can get the basilica towers rising right behind the Cloth Hall roofline.
card.good_to_know: The square dates back to the 13th century and covers about 4 hectares, often described as one of the largest medieval town squares in Europe. The Cloth Hall was rebuilt in the Renaissance style after a fire in 1555, and its arcades were added in the 19th century. The whole Old Town has been on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1978.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the northeast corner of the square, where Floriańska Street meets Rynek Główny. Face into the square and you'll see St Mary's Basilica and the Cloth Hall (Sukiennice) sitting together in one frame, the classic postcard view.

card.hook: Step off Krakow's buzzing market square and, a few steps later, you're walking on glass over streets from seven hundred years ago. It's dim, a bit foggy and glowing, and it makes wonderfully moody photos.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the spot, where the phone icon on the map sits on the main market square. The museum is directly beneath you, partly under the Cloth Hall. Once you're inside, face along a glass walkway so it leads away from you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for most shots. Switch to 0.5x in the bigger spaces to fit in the walkways and displays, and use zoom 2x only for details in lit display cases.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the scene, like a projection or lit display, then drag it a little darker so the glow keeps its detail.
card.best_time: The light inside is the same all day, so aim for a quieter time with fewer people in your frame. Early in the day is often calmer.
card.selfie_here: Up top, stand by the small glass pyramid at the northeastern corner of the Cloth Hall, opposite St Mary's Basilica, with the museum entrance behind you. Down below, use the front camera at 0.5x on the glass-floored walkway so the medieval foundations show behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to take your photo from the square's northeastern corner, near Floriańska Street, so both the Cloth Hall and St Mary's Basilica fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the museum's rules on photography before you start shooting, and be considerate of other visitors. Skip the flash, as it bounces off the glass.

card.good_to_know: The museum opened in September 2010 and covers roughly 4,000 square metres. Look out for a reconstructed 12th-century workshop and a merchant's stall. Don't miss the huge medieval lump of lead called the "loaf", which weighs 693 kg.

card.hook: Picture one very long building sitting in the middle of a huge square, with two mismatched towers peeking over its roof. That's the Cloth Hall, and it's hard to take a bad photo of it.
card.stand_here: Stand in Rynek Główny, about 31 m from the Cloth Hall, and face it. That's a bit close for the whole building, so use this spot for the arcades and details. For the full view with St Mary's Basilica behind, walk farther back to the southwest corner of the square.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the long hall into one frame, then switch to 1x for a more natural look. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the towers or a single run of arches.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and keep the roofline level, then hold your phone upright so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, before the crowds arrive. Dusk is lovely too, when the buildings are floodlit, so switch on night mode and keep your elbows tucked in.
card.selfie_here: Step under the arches of the arcade on the square side, near the restaurant gardens. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and let the arches frame you. Most visitors pose here, so be patient for a gap.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the northeastern corner of the square, where Floriańska Street meets it, because one frame from there can include both St Mary's Basilica and the Cloth Hall.
card.rules_and_safety: The square and arcades are open public space, but the shops and the museum upstairs have their own rules. Photo rules in the upstairs gallery can vary and flash may be prohibited, so check the signs.
card.challenge: Catch both mismatched towers sitting just above the Cloth Hall's roofline, with the roofline dead level.
card.good_to_know: In the 15th century this was a major centre of international trade, with spices, silk, leather and wax coming in and textiles, lead and salt from Wieliczka going out. Under Austrian rule in the 19th century it was renovated to a design by Tomasz Pryliński. The Old Town around it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1978, and upstairs is the Sukiennice Museum with 19th-century Polish painting and sculpture.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Rynek Główny, about 31 m from the Cloth Hall, and face it. That's a bit close for the whole building, so use this spot for the arcades and details. For the full view with St Mary's Basilica behind, walk farther back to the southwest corner of the square.

card.hook: At first glance, the Old Synagogue looks more like a tiny fortress than a place of prayer. Look up at the attic wall and you'll spot loopholes, the narrow slits you'd expect on a castle.
card.stand_here: Stand on ulica Szeroka, on the open street in front of the synagogue at 24 Szeroka Street. The building lies 24 m to the east, so face east and shift along the street until you can see the north side.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole building from the street. If you can't step back far enough to get the roofline and entrance in, tap 0.5x and keep the building away from the edges so it doesn't look stretched. Try 2x or more (depending on your phone) for the arcades and the jagged gallery roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, hold your phone level so the walls don't lean, and put the roofline on the upper grid line with a bit of street left at the bottom.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives you softer light and fewer people in your shot. The street looks good at any time of day, though.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the small park east of the main entrance, stand on the paths with the eastern wall behind you, and use the front camera at 0.5x for more wall in the shot. You'll get the wall rather than the whole building, so it's a quieter, more historical backdrop. The bench on Szeroka Street is a relaxed second choice for a portrait, but I can't promise the synagogue will be in the frame.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Szeroka Street in line with the synagogue's facade so the whole building fits, and stand in front of it yourself; mornings are the quietest.
card.rules_and_safety: The street and the outside of the building are public. Inside, photos are allowed without flash and are fine in the prayer hall, but some exhibition rooms are restricted, so check the museum's official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get the roofline sitting perfectly on a grid line and spot the loopholes in the attic wall in the same shot?
card.good_to_know: This is the oldest synagogue building still standing in Poland. Sources disagree on when it was first built, anywhere from 1407 to 1570, but it was rebuilt in 1570 by the Italian architect Mateo Gucci. Since 1958 it has been a branch of the Historical Museum of Kraków, focused on the city's Jewish history.

card.hook: Everyone queues up on Floriańska Street for the same shot of this gate, and half of them end up with a stranger's elbow in the frame. Here's a calmer way to do it.
card.stand_here: Stand on ulica Pijarska at the gap in the surviving wall fragments, where the side street runs past the gate. Face the tower so you can see the whole thing, with far fewer people in the shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x. If the whole tower won't fit, tap 0.5x. Save zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the helmet or the dark, rough stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line one vertical edge of the tower up with a line so the walls don't lean, then tap the stonework and slide it a touch darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning is best, when the light is soft on the stonework. Some people also like golden hour, so if you're not an early bird, go for that.
card.selfie_here: Go to Floriańska Street and face south toward the Main Market Square and St. Mary's Basilica, with the gate at your back. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone upright so the tower rises over your shoulder. Arrive early for fewer people.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the gap in the wall fragments on Pijarska Street, where the whole tower fits in the frame, while you pose in front of the gate.
card.rules_and_safety: The area feels safe, but pickpockets sometimes blend into crowds, so keep your bag zipped. The gate's upper gallery and wall walk need a paid ticket, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the stone eagle on the north face and the relief of St. Florian on the south face, and get a photo of both.
card.good_to_know: This is the only one of Kraków's original eight medieval city gates that wasn't dismantled in the 19th century. It was first mentioned in 1307 and was part of the defences built after the Tatar attack of 1241. The tower is 33.5 metres tall, with a Baroque metal helmet from 1660 on top, and the Royal Route to Wawel Castle starts right here.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on ulica Pijarska at the gap in the surviving wall fragments, where the side street runs past the gate. Face the tower so you can see the whole thing, with far fewer people in the shot.

card.hook: Picture a giant red-brown drum wearing seven tiny pointed hats, parked at the edge of the Old Town. That's the Barbican, and it's hard to take a bad photo of it.
card.stand_here: Stand on Basztowa, the street beside the Barbican that's lined with historic townhouses. Face the fortress so the townhouses run down one side and lead your eye to it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole round fortress and the townhouses beside it. If the turrets or the moat edge get cut off, try zoom 0.5x. Zoom 2x or more is great for close shots of the turrets and brickwork.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the Barbican just off-centre, then tap the brick wall and slide the brightness down a touch so the sky stays blue and the brick keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light that flatters the brick, and fewer people wander into your frame. The outside views work all year.
card.selfie_here: Try Floriańska Street: turn so you're facing the Old Town square and the Barbican sits behind you in the distance. Use the front camera, hold the phone a little higher than usual, and tilt it slightly up so the turrets stay in the shot. You can also try the Planty park path beside the pond that looks across at the Barbican.
card.ask_someone: In Planty Park, find the angle that shows the turrets in full profile and ask a passer-by to take your photo there with the Barbican behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the outside from the public street. The inside is run as a museum site, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Count the turrets in your photo. Can you get all seven in one shot without chopping off the base?
card.good_to_know: The Barbican was built around 1498 as an outpost in front of Kraków's city walls, and it once checked everyone coming into the city. It's described as one of only three such fortified outposts still standing in Europe, and the best preserved. The walls are about 3 metres thick with 130 narrow openings for defenders, and in 1817 two senators talked the city out of demolishing it.

card.hook: Seventy oversized metal chairs stand in tidy rows on a plain grey square, all facing the same way, with ordinary city life carrying on right behind them. It's quiet, strange and very photogenic.
card.stand_here: Walk in among the chairs in Plac Bohaterów Getta, in Podgórze, until you reach the phone icon on the map. Then face across the paved square so the whole grid fills your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the chairs. Go to zoom 0.5x to fit the whole square in, but keep it close to the chairs because it stretches the edges. Try zoom 2x, if your phone has it, to pull a few rows together.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the rows of chairs with them, then tap a chair and nudge the picture a little darker so the grey paving keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon. The light is softer and there are fewer people in the square.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside one of the smaller chairs at the tram stop on the edge of the square, with the wider square and its big chairs behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and keep it simple and respectful.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand near the old German guardhouse at the north end of the square while you stand with the chairs spread out behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a place of remembrance, so keep your photos respectful and don't point your phone at other visitors. Skip the flash.
card.challenge: Find two frames with everyday city life in them: rows of chairs in front of the small historic police box, and the chairs along the eastern edge with the tram stop canopy behind.
card.good_to_know: The square was once called Mały Rynek, which means Small Market Square. Between 1941 and 1943 it lay inside the Kraków Ghetto and was a gathering point for Jewish residents before deportation. The memorial was unveiled after the square was redeveloped in 2005. Its designers, Piotr Lewicki and Kazimierz Łatak, took their idea from Tadeusz Pankiewicz's account of furniture being carried out into the square as the houses were cleared.

card.hook: Picture a smooth green dome rising over a huge open meadow, with the Old Town towers poking into the same view. That's the Kościuszko Mound, and from far away it looks surprisingly tiny until you zoom in.
card.stand_here: Stand in Błonia, the broad meadow on the mound's lower side. The mound lies to the south-west, about 1.1 km away, so face that way and you'll see it rise above the grass.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch the whole scene, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the mound and the Old Town towers closer. Skip 0.5x for the mound itself, because it will look very small. It's better for the meadow and sky.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the mound on one of the upper lines and let the meadow fill the bottom third.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day. Early morning or the hour before sunset gives you softer light.
card.selfie_here: Try the grass meadow just below the mound, on the path up from the Wolski/Salwator side. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the mound over your shoulder. Sources are thin on selfies here, so check the framing on the spot.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone on the open Błonia meadows and stand with the mound in the background across the park.
card.rules_and_safety: The path to the top has no guard rail and steep sides, so keep a close eye on children near the edges. If you want to climb the mound, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get the mound, the Old Town towers and a big slice of meadow all in one shot? Crouch a little to make the hill look taller.
card.good_to_know: Cracovians raised the mound in memory of Tadeusz Kościuszko, and it was finished in November 1823. People of all ages and classes helped build it, and it stands about 35 metres high. It was modelled on Kraków's ancient mounds of Krak and Wanda.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Błonia, the broad meadow on the mound's lower side. The mound lies to the south-west, about 1.1 km away, so face that way and you'll see it rise above the grass.

card.hook: Kraków pulled down its whole Town Hall in 1820, and this one tower just stayed put, leaning by 55 centimetres since a storm in 1703. That small tilt is why it looks friendlier than a stiff, perfectly upright tower.
card.stand_here: Stand in Rynek Główny (the Main Market Square), on the south side of the square, looking north-northwest at the tower. From there it rises over the square with its slight lean showing against the Old Town rooftops.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the whole tower fits with some rooftops and sky around it. Go to 0.5x only when you're close and want the stone lions and the doorway in one shot. If your phone has zoom 2x, use it for a tighter shot of the top of the tower without walking closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line, so the lean is easy to spot.
card.best_time: Go early if you can, as it's usually calmer and fewer people will wander through your frame. This is an outdoor, ground-level shot, so daylight is all you need.
card.selfie_here: Try the bronze Eros Bendato head, in the south-western corner of Rynek Główny at the foot of the tower. Use the front camera at arm's length, stand beside the head, and turn so the tower is over your shoulder. Tap your face so you stay bright.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the south side of the square facing north-northwest, while you stand in front of the tower so the lean shows behind you; the Cloth Hall or St Mary's towers can sneak into the frame too.
card.rules_and_safety: A local guide advised against climbing inside the Eros Bendato head, because late-night revellers leaving the pubs have been known to use it as a toilet. Pose beside it instead.
card.challenge: Find the two stone lions guarding the entrance, then get one of them and the Gothic portal with the city coat of arms above the door in a single frame.
card.good_to_know: The tower is all that's left of the old Town Hall, which came down in 1820 to open up the Main Market Square. It was built at the end of the 14th century in stone and brick and stands 70 metres tall. The observation deck at the top is an indoor, ticketed view, so check the official site if you want to go up.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Rynek Główny (the Main Market Square), on the south side of the square, looking north-northwest at the tower. From there it rises over the square with its slight lean showing against the Old Town rooftops.

card.hook: Most spots give you one photo. Collegium Maius gives you two: a quiet street corner with a pointy Gothic gable, and a brick courtyard with a well in the middle. Grab both if you can.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of ulica Jagiellońska and ulica Świętej Anny, right at the oldest stone part of the college. The main part of the building is to the west, about 1 minute on foot, so face west towards it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x, which helps if you're close and want the whole gable and bay window in. Then try 1x for a natural look, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for details of the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the edge of the building with a vertical line so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or a softer, overcast day should give you the quietest street and the gentlest light on the stone. The courtyard is likely to be busier around the middle of the day.
card.selfie_here: Head into the arcaded courtyard and stand next to the central well, with the Gothic arches behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a bit low, and let the arches fill the background. The antique Professors' Stairs in the courtyard are another good backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to take your photo while you stand on the pavement on Jagiellońska Street in front of the street-side facade, with the corner of St Anne Street in view.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally fine in the courtyard, but inside the museum check the signs or ask staff, as rules vary by room. Flash is generally discouraged or banned near the scientific instruments and fragile manuscripts.
card.challenge: Take one tall photo where the gable and bay window are the stars and the walls stand perfectly straight on your gridlines.
card.good_to_know: Collegium Maius is the oldest building of the Jagiellonian University, with parts dating back to the 14th century. King Władysław II Jagiełło bought it with money left by his late wife, Queen Jadwiga, and the university moved in. Nicolaus Copernicus was a student here in the 1490s, and the courtyard well was added in 1517.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of ulica Jagiellońska and ulica Świętej Anny, right at the oldest stone part of the college. The main part of the building is to the west, about 1 minute on foot, so face west towards it.

card.hook: Floriańska Street is so dead straight that it feels like someone drew it with a ruler. Stand under the old gate arch and the whole street leads your eye to the tower of St. Mary's Basilica.
card.stand_here: Stand at Brama Floriańska (St. Florian's Gate), just inside the arch on the gate's inner (south) side. Face south-west, so the street runs away from you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the straight view down the street. If you're squeezed in and the arch won't fit, tap 0.5x. Want the basilica tower bigger? Try 2x (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the street's centre in the middle of the frame, and keep your phone level so the buildings stand up straight.
card.best_time: Early morning is the usual advice, because this is a busy pedestrian street for much of the day. Wait for a gap between groups and take several shots, then pick the one with the cleanest foreground.
card.selfie_here: Try the gate at the northern end of Floriańska, near the Barbican, with the street stretching out behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the gate and street sit over your shoulder. Fair warning: this is our best guess for a selfie spot, not a famous one.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand near St. Mary's Basilica at the Main Square end and shoot back up the street, while you stand on Floriańska with St. Florian's Gate far behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The street is open and free, and standing under the gate arch costs nothing. The gate's upper parts and interior are ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Catch a clean gap in the crowd with the basilica tower dead centre. Bonus points if the arch frames it perfectly.
card.good_to_know: The street is about 335 metres long and appears on the 1257 plan of the extended city. It was part of the Royal Road, and a horse tram ran along it from 1882. Today you'll find shops, cafés and restaurants in the tall town houses, including the Jan Matejko House and the Jama Michalika café.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Brama Floriańska (St. Florian's Gate), just inside the arch on the gate's inner (south) side. Face south-west, so the street runs away from you.

card.hook: Twelve stone apostles line the fence out front, and behind them a tall, pale Baroque facade towers over Grodzka Street. It's like a very dignified queue.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plac św. Marii Magdaleny, on the open side facing Grodzka street, across from the church facade. The church is to the east of you, so face east and you'll see the facade and tower straight on.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the straight-on view of the whole facade and tower. If the square is too crowded to step back, switch to 0.5x to squeeze it all in. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for the statues in the niches and the coat of arms at the very top.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so the facade doesn't lean, and put the Piotr Skarga monument at one edge of the frame.
card.best_time: Go early or at an off-peak time. The square is small and usually busy, so you'll get a much clearer frame. If people keep wandering through, just take a few shots.
card.selfie_here: Try the church forecourt beside the apostle statues on the fence at Grodzka 52A, which puts the facade right behind you. Use the front camera, or 0.5x if you want the whole front in. Check the exact spot on the map before you go.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back on the wide open forecourt in front of the church gate while you stand by the fence, so the apostle statues and the facade both fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is an active place of worship, so check the official site before you go inside. If you do take photos in there, skip the flash, which isn't allowed because of the frescoes and paintings.
card.challenge: Get the tower perfectly straight on a gridline with Skarga tucked in the corner. Bonus points if nobody photobombs you.
card.good_to_know: The church was built between 1597 and 1619 and paid for by King Sigismund III Vasa for the Jesuits. It's described as the first building in Kraków designed entirely in the Baroque style, and it's the biggest of the city's historic churches by seating capacity. The apostle sculptures on the fence are modern copies, made to replace 18th-century originals that acid rain badly damaged.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plac św. Marii Magdaleny, on the open side facing Grodzka street, across from the church facade. The church is to the east of you, so face east and you'll see the facade and tower straight on.
